name: Pec / bicep implants

card.summary: Solid silicone implants that add chest or arm bulk surgically; little independent evidence exists on cosmetic use in healthy men.
card.note: Surgical risks apply; sources are mostly surgeon-written.

quick.overview:
Pectoral and bicep implants are solid silicone pieces placed under or around muscle to make it look bigger. Pectoral implants were first used for reconstruction and later for cosmetic chest contouring.

In looksmaxxing they sit under hardmaxxing, as a surgical alternative to training. Independent studies of cosmetic use in healthy men were not found.
quick.mechanism: The implant is inserted into a surgically created pocket, typically beneath the pectoralis major, and adds volume and shape from underneath.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, infection, hematoma or seroma, shifting, asymmetry, numbness and scarring. Silicone devices are regulated as medical devices; much of the available description comes from surgeon marketing.

lead: Pectoral and bicep implants are solid silicone prostheses placed surgically in or around a muscle to give it more volume and a more defined outline. For the chest, the implant sits in a pocket beneath the pectoralis major and adds fixed fullness that men with a flat or underdeveloped chest use to look broader and more muscular; for the arms, the same idea is applied to the biceps and other muscles such as the calves [1][2].

Pectoral implants began as a reconstructive device for chest-wall differences such as pectus excavatum and Poland syndrome, and later moved into cosmetic chest contouring [1][2]. Wikipedia describes the pectoral implant as the male counterpart of the breast prosthesis, used to correct male chest defects and deformities [1]. In looksmaxxing culture the procedure sits under hardmaxxing, as a surgical route to size and shape that training, genetics or testosterone have not delivered.

Clinic and surgeon material describes oval implants that mainly build the lower chest and vertical-rectangular shapes that also fill the upper chest, [3]. Fat grafting is the usual alternative, giving a softer, more natural fullness without sharp definition [3]. Independent controlled studies of cosmetic pectoral or bicep implants in healthy men have not been published; most descriptions come from surgeons and clinics.

Adds fixed volume and defined edges to the chest
angle.text: The implant adds volume under the skin and muscle right away, so the chest or arm looks larger and more sculpted without the months of training that muscle growth takes. People with a flat chest, one-sided underdevelopment or a lean frame with little donor fat are the groups surgeons describe it for [3].

About 1 to 2 weeks, per a clinic source [3]
Roughly 10 to 20 years without complication, per a surgeon-sourced summary [2]

paras: Unlike breast implants, which are filled with silicone gel or saline, pectoral implants are described as made of solid, medical-grade silicone elastomer. They come in rectangular or anatomical shapes and a range of volumes, and are placed in a pocket beneath the pectoralis major, commonly through an armpit incision [2][3].

A clinic source describes two common male designs: an oval implant that mainly enhances the lower chest and a vertical-rectangular implant that also fills the upper chest. Because the material is solid and firm, orientation during surgery matters, and the implant can feel closer to a flexed muscle than a relaxed one [3].
Bicep and calf implants follow the same principle of a solid silicone shape placed to increase the apparent size of the muscle, but they are much less documented than chest implants [2].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia whose content may contain errors, states that the procedure was introduced around 1988 for reconstruction in conditions such as pectus excavatum and Poland syndrome, and that a surgeon described its use for male chest contouring, including after gynecomastia, in 1991 [2]. Wikipedia mentions the pectoral implant within its breast implant article, as the prosthesis for correcting male breast defects and deformities [1].

Fat grafting uses the patient's own fat, harvested by liposuction and injected across the chest. A clinic comparison says it feels like natural tissue and adds fullness but rarely produces sharp definition, and that very lean men may lack enough donor fat [3].

For implants the same source describes soreness peaking in the first few days and easing over about two weeks, 1 to 2 weeks off work, and restriction of heavy pressing for about six weeks or longer, with the final look settling over several months [3].

General risks of implant surgery listed in the sources include bleeding, hematoma or seroma, infection, anesthesia reactions and wound-healing problems. Implant-specific problems described include shifting or rotation, visible edges, asymmetry, capsular contracture (described as less common with solid implants), numbness and muscle spasm [2][3].

Clinic sources note that the surrounding tissue can change over time, which may lead to revision, and that no published lifespan exists specifically for pectoral implants [3]. For silicone breast implants generally, Wikipedia reports rupture, capsular contracture and gel migration, and a 2021 US FDA boxed warning for those devices; these findings concern gel-filled breast implants and have not been shown to apply directly to solid pectoral implants [1].
No studies found. Information on outcomes comes from surgeon and clinic publications rather than controlled studies of cosmetic pectoral or bicep implants in healthy men [3].

The procedure appears in the hardmaxxing category alongside other implant and body-contouring surgeries, as a way to add muscle size independent of training or testosterone. Looksmaxxing and lifting forums discuss chest size mostly in terms of bench-press numbers and physique, and public discussion of implants specifically is limited.
